item.content:encoded:
It is sort of amazing just how different the acquisition of Luis Robert Jr. looks in October than it did in January. Robert was brought in to play center field and be an offensive upgrade over Tyrone Taylor. Even though a lot of the underlying tools looked problematic, the possibility of 25+ HR power, elite center field defense, and above average speed was an enticing mix.
Unfortunately, like has been the case with Robert for much of his career, injuries got in the way. Robert was on the injured list with back issues from April 30 to July 20. And the team that he came back to was a very, very different one from the one he left.
Specifically, the team he returned to had A.J. Ewing manning center field and doing his best Luis Robert impression.
In 58 games for the Mets, Robert hit .223/.303/.399 with 10 home runs, while playing a good center field. Ewing played just about twice as many games as Robert did, and he hit .252/.324/.376 with 11 home runs. Ewing was not a perfect player for the Mets this year, and his age and inexperience showed. He has a lot of work to do on his game, but his natural abilities, especially his speed on both sides of the ball, presented a player that has looks like he may be able to grow into what Robert has been at his best, and do so for the league minimum salary.
When Robert returned from the IL, Ewing was already firmly ensconced as the everyday center fielder, and it looked like Robert wasn't long for the team. While they couldn't find a trade partner for him, he was claimed off of waivers by the Orioles in August. With a $20 million option on the table, the Mets just didn't have a need for Robert as a fourth outfielder, and the team wasn't going to put him on the depth chart ahead of Ewing.
It is a shame how his story with the Mets ended, because Robert looked like a fantastic fit for the club: some real power, decent speed on the basepaths, and bona fide elite center field defense. But you can't blame the team for prioritizing developing a young player versus overpaying an older one, and that's exactly what the Mets did.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees enter this offseason with a glaring hole in center field that free agency will not fill. The front office needs a solution now, but the available names on the market look weak. According to Yahoo Sports, the team simply does not have many options to sign as free agents. This reality forces the club to look elsewhere for help.
Internal fixes have failed to work over the last two years. Austin Wells at catcher for example has shown great skills with his glove, but his bat has struggled to find a rhythm. The team also tried rookie Spencer Jones, who looked fresh but posted a minus-4 Outs Above Average metric in center field. That number was only a slight improvement over the minus-6 mark recorded by veteran Trent Grisham. Per Yahoo Sports, the defensive regression at this key position has become a major problem for the roster.
The Free Agent Trap
Most teams would look to the open market to fix a defensive gap. The Yankees cannot do that this time. The best available players come with heavy baggage. Daulton Varsho cannot hit well enough to justify the cost, and Luis Robert Jr. is known for being injury-prone while also lacking consistent offense. Even if Grisham returns, he should only play a corner spot, not center. Reports note that his glove has regressed since his bat finally improved in New York.
This lack of viable names means the Yankees must be creative. They cannot just wait for a deal to happen. The team needs to make a move that others might think is too risky. A trade is the only way to get a player who can actually play center field every day.
The Cruz Connection
Oneil Cruz stands out as the most logical target for this difficult task. He is a charismatic left-handed hitter who was named after Paul O'Neill. The Yankees have been linked to Cruz for years, with reports dating back to the summer of 2025. Nothing came of those talks then, but the interest never really went away. Yahoo Sports reports that the front office has targeted Cruz for a minimum of two years.
Getting him will not be easy. Reports suggest that the Pittsburgh Pirates might require some serious prying to part ways with their star. The Yankees have the assets to make a deal work, but they must act fast. Waiting too long could let another team step in and claim him. The clock is ticking on this specific opportunity to fix the roster.
Historical Context
The need for a true center fielder is not new for this franchise. Brett Gardner was probably the best the team had in the last 20 years before he retired after the 2021 season. A dropped fly ball during Game 5 of the 2024 World Series ended center field duties for Aaron Judge, despite his status as an elite player. The team has tried many names, but none have solved the issue for a full season.

item.content:encoded:
New York Mets owner Steve Cohen made it clear to the team's broadcast booth in a recent interview that the organization intends on bringing in some new voices to the front office this offseason. That's because president of baseball operations David Stearns and the current regime had a poor year in 2026.
"We're going to try to add certain voices into the front office that I think will be helpful," Cohen said. "I know David supports that and I'm looking forward to, when we make those decisions, announcing it."
While it would make sense for the Mets to bring in a general manager to work as Stearns' No. 2, Cohen said that doesn't necessarily need to be the case.
"It doesn't have to be a GM," Cohen said. "It could be other ways to support David and the front office."
So, whether it's a GM or not, the Mets will be bringing in new perspectives this winter to assist Stearns and the front office. And once that happens, here's the advice this new voice/s should give Stearns and co.
Advice to Mets baseball head honcho David Stearns
This should be an easy one as it was Stearns' biggest blunder of the year; Don't rely on injury prone/aging players. Stearns brought in the likes of Jorge Polanco, Luis Robert Jr. and Marcus Semien as new faces to replace franchise mainstays: Pete Alonso, Brandon Nimmo and Jeff McNeil.
This strategy proved to be a big mistake given all three new acquisitions missed time due to injury this year and greatly underperformed. Not to mention, the trio Stearns let go of all play everyday and rarely miss time each year. The new GM or voice/s should be advising Stearns to re-evaluate how he views durability/reliability when it comes to player acquisition. Polanco and Robert already had reputations for being injury prone in their careers.
The Mets cannot go into another season relying on Polanco to play first base (coming off ankle surgery) or Semien (36-years-old) to play second base. Both players are making a good bit of money next season, but the Mets shouldn't force them to be full-time players when they aren't reliable. Robert was claimed off waivers by the Baltimore Orioles, so the Mets are no longer on the hook for his $2 million buyout.
The new voice/s should be helping Stearns pull off creative trades and find low-risk, high-reward veteran options that can produce for the Mets next season. The Mets had the second-highest payroll in baseball behind the Los Angeles Dodgers, but had a disastrous year. It clearly makes sense for them to bring some new voices into the fold for next season and beyond.

item.content:encoded:
The Mets have just nine games left in the season, and all of the attention is already shifting to the 2027 campaign. There are a lot of questions that the Mets have to answer this winter, and seeing the fans' over-the-top reaction to Pete Alonso's return this week shows how much work the front office needs to do to win back the trust of its fan base.
The free agent market is a bit thin this year, but it does have a few players who could help the Mets bolster their roster, particularly in the pitching department. That tally doesn't include Bo Bichette, whose opt-out decision will also play a significant role in how much money President of Baseball Operations David Stearns has to work with in free agency.
That said, let's dive into five potential free agents that the Mets should pursue this winter.
1. LHP Tarik Skubal
We took a deeper dive into the Tarik Skubal fit for the Mets last week, but it is fair to wonder if the fans' vitriolic display at Citi Field this week may inspire Steve Cohen to go for the top pitcher on the board as a make-good to them.
There are certainly injury risks with Skubal, but there isn't a better pitcher on the board, and his arrival would push the rest of the current rotation into more appropriate roles, starting with Nolan McLean as one of the best No. 2's in baseball.
2. LHP Robbie Ray
Skubal alone would bolster the Mets' rotation but Stearns should also look to add a veteran for the middle of the rotation who can give them quality innings. Enter Robbie Ray, a former Cy Young winner who is 13-8 with a 3.60 ERA in 30 appearances (including 29 starts) between the Giants and Padres.
The Mets would get a veteran lefty who has thrown at least 162.2 innings in four of the past six seasons, with the only exceptions being the 2022 and 2023 campaigns when he missed significant time rehabbing from Tommy John surgery. Putting Ray as the Mets' third starter would allow Stearns to bump Christian Scott down to the No. 4 spot and have healthy competition for the fifth between Sean Manaea, Jonah Tong, Zac Thornton and a slew of other depth options.
3. 1B/3B Alec Bohm
First base is one of the bigger questions on the Mets' roster, and they can't go into next season hoping that the combination of Jared Young, Mark Vientos, Brett Baty and Jorge Polanco can solve it. One good fit here could be Alec Bohm, who is hitting .251 with 15 home runs, 84 RBIs and a .707 OPS in 534 at-bats for the Phillies.
If the Mets feel like Young can be part of a first base platoon, then Bohm would make sense as a partner since he is very strong against lefties, batting .293 with seven homers, 36 RBIs and an .828 OPS against them in 179 at-bats. Veteran Paul Goldschmidt could also fill a platoon role with Young, but the Mets would be better served going with someone in his prime as opposed to a Goldschmidt-type towards the end of his career.
Bohm's ability to play both infield corners could also be helpful in the event Bichette opts out.
4. OF Ramon Laureano
The Mets' decision to move on from Tyrone Taylor (via trade) and Luis Robert Jr. (via waivers) has left them with an all-left-handed-hitting outfield of Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge. While all three are capable starters, it would make sense to add a veteran option who can hit right-handed since Nick Morabito appears to need more minor league seasoning to be ready for that fourth outfielder role.
A good buy-low fit here could be Ramón Laureano, who has missed most of the season after undergoing surgery to repair a torn labrum in his right hip in May. Laureano can play both outfield corners and is just a year removed from a solid 2025 campaign where he hit .281 with 24 homers, 76 RBIs and an .855 OPS, so adding him on a one-year prove-it deal could give the Mets more flexibility to protect Juan Soto's health with DH days or sit one of Ewing or Benge against tough lefties.
5. RHP Evan Phillips
The Mets bullpen's strong performance post-deadline has lessened their need to go big-game hunting at the back end of the unit, but they still need to add a proven setup reliever to their mix. One name who could offer good value is Evan Phillips, who has pitched to a 3.68 ERA and 1.23 WHIP in 27 appearances for the Dodgers this season.
Phillips missed time with injuries this year but does have closing experience with Los Angeles, which could be valuable if Devin Williams struggles in his second year with the Mets. The injury issues Phillips had may drive his price down to a one- or two-year contract, which would be right up Stearns' wheelhouse and make him a good complement to the likes of Williams, Kodai Senga, Reed Garrett and Daniel Duarte in the relief mix.
